Public-interest evidence audit · 26 July 2026

JAOC’s “AI-Generated Photograph” Claim

A technical and credibility audit of the dossier being used to attack Nigel Farage for sharing a photograph published across the national media.

Prepared for Reform UK administrators and senior officialsPrepared for circulation by Steve EnglishVersion 1.0
Read the verdict
Legal and editorial note: Criminal proceedings are active. This report refers to Joshua Kerry as the defendant or man charged, makes no finding of guilt, and examines only JAOC’s image-authenticity claim and the credibility of its published methodology.
Executive finding

JAOC has not proved that the photograph was generated by AI.

Its published dossier is not a reproducible forensic examination. Several of its central technical claims are demonstrably wrong, logically invalid or contradicted by the public record.

The proper conclusion is not that the photograph has been conclusively authenticated. The proper conclusion is narrower and decisive: JAOC has supplied no competent basis for declaring it synthetic, for accusing the national media of knowingly or negligently circulating an AI portrait, or for saying Nigel Farage should have recognised it as fake.

UnsupportedAI-generation claim

No original file, validated AI marker, detector result or source-platform evidence.

Contradicted“No source credit” claim

The Sun credits the image to itself; the Guardian credits The Sun.

Not demonstrated“Peer-reviewed” status

No reviewer, credentials, review notes or independent report are identified.

UnresolvedExact original provenance

The first camera file and company post were not available to this audit.

1. Scope and evidence examined

This audit tests whether JAOC’s published evidence justifies its public conclusion that the photograph is “almost certainly AI-generated”. It also examines whether the organisation’s presentation gives readers a misleading impression of professional forensic or intelligence authority.

Material examined included:

  • JAOC’s “Image Authenticity Dossier”, document reference DOSS-AUTH-2026-0722, Revision 2, dated 22 July 2026.
  • JAOC’s published collage of an ordinary photograph, a charity-fundraiser photograph and outputs from the free browser tool Forensically.
  • The image files supplied with the dossier material, including an 800 × 787 WebP derivative and the assembled contact sheet.
  • JAOC’s home page, transparency statement, editorial charter, disclaimer, investigation index and claims about its operational reach.
  • Publications by The Sun, The Guardian and other outlets, along with primary technical documentation from Adobe, IPTC, Forensically and INTERPOL.
Important limitation: This audit did not receive the original camera file or the original social-media upload from the former employer. Without that source material, neither JAOC nor this audit can perform a definitive camera-origin examination. That uncertainty does not turn into proof of AI generation.

2. What JAOC claims

JAOC’s dossier states that the image was first publicly traceable in mid-July 2026 and then declares that it is synthetic, “not captured by a physical camera”, anonymously mass-distributed and published without valid attribution. It says a UUID is a generation marker, missing EXIF is suspicious, visual filters reveal anomalies, and the absence of cloned regions confirms that all elements were generated from scratch.

“No cloned sections detected — confirming all elements were generated from scratch.”

That sentence is the clearest single example of the dossier’s problem. An ordinary unedited photograph would also normally contain no copied-and-pasted sections. A negative clone-detection result cannot distinguish an authentic photograph from an AI-generated image.

The dossier also labels itself “peer-reviewed” and attributes its production to an “Image Forensics Division”, while disclosing no named examiner, reviewer, qualifications, laboratory process or raw evidence.

3. The screenshots do not detect AI

3.1 The software’s creator expressly warns against this use

The interface shown is Forensically, a free browser-based set of image-inspection tools created by Jonas Wagner. Its own documentation describes it as a magnifying glass and says it cannot decide whether something is true or false. The clone detector is described as an early, imperfect tool, and the error-level results are explicitly said to be capable of misleading the user.

JAOC presents screenshots from a tool whose own author warns that it does not deliver the conclusion JAOC assigns to it.

3.2 Clone detection

Clone detection searches for similar blocks that may indicate copy-and-paste editing. Repeated office features—blinds, ceiling tiles, papers, walls, furniture edges and compression blocks—can produce numerous matches. The purple marks and red connecting lines in the JAOC collage are therefore not proof of synthesis.

More importantly, JAOC’s written claim is backwards: finding no cloned regions does not confirm generation from scratch. It merely means that this detector, at those undisclosed settings and on that web derivative, did not identify a copy-move pattern.

3.3 Level sweep, luminance gradients and PCA

These tools exaggerate brightness ranges, edges, channel differences, noise and compression artefacts. They may help a trained examiner notice an area requiring further investigation. They do not independently classify an image as AI-generated, and JAOC provides no control images showing how the same settings behave on known camera photographs and known AI images.

3.4 Error-level and noise analysis

Repeated resizing and JPEG/WebP conversion can alter error and noise patterns throughout an image. The Forensically documentation specifically warns that such results become unreliable when an image has been resized or heavily compressed—the exact conditions expected for pictures copied between employers, social media, news desks and content-delivery networks.

4. The metadata claims fail

4.1 A UUID is not an AI-generation fingerprint

JAOC reproduces a truncated identifier beginning urn:uuid: and labels it a “generation-specific” marker. Adobe’s official XMP Media Management specification says ordinary files may contain UUID-based DocumentID and InstanceID values; an instance identifier can be updated whenever a file is saved. A UUID therefore shows that some software assigned an identifier. By itself, it says nothing about whether the pixels were produced by a camera, Photoshop, a content-management system or a generative model.

JAOC does not publish the full metadata block, the field name, namespace, surrounding values, extraction command, software version or file hash. It also lists “cross-reference the UUID against known AI generation platforms” as future work—after already declaring the image synthetic.

The dossier reaches its conclusion before carrying out the test that it says might connect the UUID to an AI platform.

4.2 Missing EXIF is normal in web derivatives

The absence of camera make, capture time, GPS and photographer information is not evidence that no camera existed. IPTC—the standards body for news-photo metadata—has documented that websites, social platforms, resizing systems and content-management workflows frequently remove embedded metadata. IPTC also warns that CMS and CDN tools may strip metadata during cropping and manipulation.

The supplied WebP derivative and JAOC’s assembled JPEG contact sheet contain no useful EXIF. That is consistent with web processing; it cannot reconstruct the state of the original file.

4.3 Proper AI provenance uses identifiable attestations, not guesswork

Modern provenance systems such as C2PA can carry signed content credentials and AI-related attestations. JAOC publishes no C2PA manifest, recognised AI DigitalSourceType, generator name, model identifier, prompt record or platform signature. Its UUID assertion is not a substitute.

5. Provenance and media publication

5.1 JAOC’s “no credit line” statement is contradicted

The Sun’s 18 July article captions the photograph with the credit “The Sun” and describes it as showing the defendant holding Easter eggs during a charity fundraiser. The Guardian’s 20 July report labels the image “Photograph: The Sun”.

That does not identify the original photographer, and The Sun should still be able to explain its acquisition route. It does, however, directly disprove JAOC’s categorical statement that no outlet displayed a valid credit or source disclosure.

5.2 Secondary reports describe a real workplace fundraiser

Several publications describe the image as originating from a 2022 workplace charity fundraiser for local Sea Cadets and a social-media post by colleagues. This is a plausible provenance trail, but the original employer post was not located in this audit and should still be obtained. The responsible wording is therefore: reported workplace provenance, not yet independently closed.

5.3 “Official media portrait” is a straw man

A newsroom photograph does not have to be issued by police, a court or the Crown Prosecution Service to be genuine. Newspapers routinely obtain lawful pictures from employers, family contacts, public social-media pages, agencies and their own reporters. JAOC moves from “not shown to be an official police handout” to “not a photograph captured by a camera”. Those are completely different propositions.

5.4 The “unrelated article” theory is unproved

JAOC says the image appeared on old baking, rugby, reality-TV and other unrelated pages and infers that it was injected into automated publishing systems. A much simpler possibility is that those pages contained dynamic “latest news”, “most read” or recommendation modules. Reverse-image search engines can associate an image with any page where it is rendered, including a sidebar card that changes over time.

JAOC supplies no archived page captures proving that the photograph was used as the lead or inline editorial image for each unrelated story. Without that evidence, its “random injection” narrative remains speculation.

6. Why the dossier is not a forensic report

A professional conclusion of this seriousness should be independently reproducible. JAOC’s document lacks the fundamentals:

  • No original file: only downstream web copies appear to have been examined.
  • No chain of custody: no record of who obtained each file, from where, when or how it was preserved.
  • No cryptographic file hash in the report: readers cannot know which exact file produced each screenshot.
  • No complete metadata dump: a truncated UUID is shown without its field or context.
  • No software audit trail: versions, settings and exports are omitted.
  • No control set: no known camera images and known generated images are run through the same process.
  • No quantified result: no validated detector score, confidence interval, false-positive rate or decision threshold.
  • No named examiner: qualifications and relevant experience are absent.
  • No identified peer reviewer: “peer-reviewed” is asserted rather than demonstrated.
  • No completed provenance enquiries: picture-desk questions are postponed to the recommendations section.
Correct evidential standard: The person making the extraordinary claim must provide affirmative, reproducible evidence of synthesis. The burden is not satisfied by pointing to missing data in a repeatedly processed web copy.

7. JAOC’s wider credibility and organisational presentation

7.1 The visible operation is highly person-centred

JAOC’s transparency statement switches to the first person: Andrew says he personally pays the costs, takes no salary, sold his home, uses savings and works on JAOC seven days a week. That may be entirely sincere, but it sits uneasily beside institutional branding such as “Threat Intelligence Unit”, “Image Forensics Division”, operational cells and extensive undercover teams.

No conventional masthead was found listing an editor, reporters, technical specialists, forensic examiner, legal adviser or review board. The public cannot test the claimed division of labour or expertise.

7.2 Extraordinary operational claims lack disclosed corroboration

The site claims undercover reach inside the civil service, political parties, MPs’ offices, Companies House senior management, corporations, NGOs, diplomatic circles and UK “special services”. It also describes collaboration with INTERPOL and covert cross-border work. These claims are not accompanied by authenticated correspondence, named officials, operation references, court exhibits or independent reporting sufficient to verify them.

INTERPOL’s own public guidance says it does not conduct investigations or arrests; those functions remain with national police. A private citizen can send information to police, but that is very different from operating an INTERPOL-linked investigative unit.

7.3 Website-safety scores are presented as journalism accreditation

JAOC advertises a ScamAdviser score as evidence of unmatched credibility and ranks itself against private investigation businesses. ScamAdviser’s own methodology says its score is an automated risk indicator, not a verdict, designed chiefly to help consumers assess whether a site may be malicious, fraudulent or unsafe to transact with. SSL, domain age and hosting signals do not verify reporting, sources or forensic competence.

7.4 Editorial certainty and legal disclaimers conflict

JAOC’s editorial charter promises meticulous, cross-checked, evidence-led reporting. Its terms and disclaimer meanwhile say content may contain errors and is not an authoritative statement of fact. Disclaimers are normal, but the contrast matters when the site markets a categorical “confirmed” forensic conclusion while withholding the evidence required to reproduce it.

7.5 Reputation outside JAOC’s own ecosystem

Searches found JAOC’s own pages, social-media appearances, forums, user testimonials and material it hosts. No established pattern was found of major newsrooms, recognised investigative organisations or courts relying on JAOC as a forensic or intelligence authority. Absence of mainstream citation does not prove an investigation wrong; it does mean JAOC has not demonstrated the professional standing implied by its branding.

7.6 What this audit does not allege

There is insufficient evidence to accuse Andrew Sibley of stealing donations, operating a financial fraud or knowingly fabricating every investigation. JAOC says donations are used for hosting and infrastructure and that Andrew receives no salary. Those financial claims have not been audited here. Criticism should remain on the strongest ground: the published methods and evidence do not support the authority claimed.

9. Recommended response for Reform UK

  1. Do not repeat JAOC’s AI claim as fact. It is unsupported and risks spreading misinformation during active criminal proceedings.
  2. Circulate this audit to group owners and senior administrators. Posts featuring JAOC’s claim should be removed, paused or clearly labelled as unverified until primary evidence is produced.
  3. Preserve evidence. Save the current JAOC dossier, page, social-media videos, captions and publication dates before material changes.
  4. Ask The Sun’s picture desk for provenance. Request the acquisition source, original caption, date, file history and whether the former employer’s social-media post can be identified.
  5. Invite JAOC to answer the technical questions below. A genuine forensic operation should be able to supply them promptly.
  6. Avoid personal abuse and financial allegations. The strongest rebuttal is factual: the report is technically defective and its conclusion is not established.
  7. Use legally careful language. Refer to “the defendant” or “the man charged”, and avoid commentary that could prejudice the trial.
Suggested internal summary:
“JAOC’s report does not prove that the photograph was AI-generated. It misrepresents ordinary UUID metadata, treats missing EXIF in a web copy as evidence, draws an invalid conclusion from clone detection, supplies no original file or named peer reviewer, and is contradicted by published image credits. Reform groups should not amplify the allegation unless JAOC produces reproducible primary evidence.”

10. Questions JAOC must answer

A credible response requires documents and raw outputs, not another narrative statement.

  1. What exact file was examined? Publish its filename, byte size, SHA-256 hash and acquisition source.
  2. Was it the original camera file, an employer social-media download, a newspaper CDN derivative or a screenshot?
  3. Publish the complete EXIF, IPTC, XMP, JPEG/WebP structure and strings output—not a truncated UUID.
  4. What exact metadata field and namespace contained the UUID?
  5. Which AI platform allegedly creates that field, and where is the platform documentation proving it?
  6. Which software and versions were used, and what settings produced every screenshot?
  7. Publish the raw Forensically outputs and equivalent runs on known authentic and known AI control images.
  8. Which validated AI-image detector was used, what score was returned, and what is its documented false-positive rate?
  9. Who conducted the examination? Provide the examiner’s name, qualifications and relevant case experience.
  10. Who performed the claimed peer review? Publish the reviewer’s name, qualifications and written review.
  11. What enquiries were made to The Sun, the former employer, the charity or the local Sea Cadets before publication?
  12. Where are the archived screenshots proving the image was used as editorial content on unrelated old articles rather than in dynamic recommendation modules?
  13. Why did the dossier declare a conclusion before completing its own recommended UUID cross-check and picture-desk enquiries?
  14. Has any AI system helped draft the analysis or interpret the outputs? If so, identify the system and human verification process.

11. Final conclusion

JAOC’s report is best described as pseudo-forensic presentation: genuine technical terms and colourful filter outputs arranged around a conclusion they do not prove.

The dossier’s decisive points fail under basic scrutiny. A UUID is not an AI fingerprint. Missing EXIF in a web derivative is routine. No detected cloning cannot prove generation from scratch. The free software shown is not an AI detector. The report gives no source file, chain of custody, full metadata, reproducible workflow, named examiner or identifiable peer reviewer. Its claim that no publisher supplied a credit is contradicted by The Sun and The Guardian.

JAOC may still uncover useful documents in other work, and its founder may sincerely believe his conclusions. Sincerity, however, is not a substitute for evidence. Until JAOC supplies the primary materials listed above, Reform UK officials and group administrators should treat the AI allegation—and the attack on Nigel Farage built upon it—as unsubstantiated.
